Prepare for your cancer visit

A clear diagnosis, a treatment goal, and questions you can take into the room.

Questions for my team

Editorial update · October 26, 2026

Educational summary prepared with AI assistance from the linked sources. Individual clinical review of this guide has not yet been documented. Approval of the poster collection does not extend to this page.

Take one step at a time

A new diagnosis can feel overwhelming. You do not have to remember every medical term or ask every question at once. Choose the questions that matter most to you, bring someone you trust if you wish, and ask your team to explain anything that is unclear.

Start with the report

A pathology report describes the tissue examined and the diagnosis. Grade describes how abnormal the cells look. Stage describes the extent of cancer. Biomarker results may guide treatment, and some results arrive later as an addendum. Ask your team which findings are final and which are still pending.

What changes the plan

The cancer type, extent, biology, prior treatment, overall health and your priorities shape the discussion. Ask your clinician to explain the goal before comparing options. A list of drugs is not an individualized treatment sequence.

Questions for your next visit

Bring what helps

Bring your medication list, outside reports, and your three most important questions. Ask whether a support person or interpreter can join. Request a written summary of the agreed next step.

A learning example

Hypothetical example, not a patient story. Two reports can name the same organ but contain different tumor types or biomarkers. A useful question is “Which finding in my report changes the options?”

If symptoms cannot wait

Follow your treatment team’s urgent-symptom instructions. Call 911 for severe breathing difficulty, new stroke symptoms or another life-threatening emergency.
